transitivity: both — transitive (*grifted his own fans*), intransitive (*he has been grifting for years*)
gloss: To make money by cheating people, usually with a convincing story.
examples: Con artists *grift* the elderly by phone every single day.
He *grifted* thousands of dollars out of his own supporters.
She realized the coach had been *grifting* the whole time.

gloss: To twist your face for a moment because of pain, disgust, or annoyance.
examples: Try not to *grimace* when you taste it.
He *grimaced* and grabbed his knee.
She was *grimacing* through the last mile of the race.
contrast: The stress falls on the first syllable in American English: GRIM-uhs, not gri-MAYS.

gloss: To complain in a steady, low-level, annoying way about small things.
examples: The players *gripe* about the practice schedule every year.
He *griped* that the coffee was cold again.
They spent the whole drive *griping* about traffic.
contrast: You *gripe* **about** something; drop the -e before -ing: griping, not gripeing.

gloss: To press your teeth tightly together, usually to get through pain or anger.
examples: *Grit* your teeth — this will only take a second.
He *gritted* his teeth and kept walking on the broken ankle.
She answered politely, *gritting* her teeth the whole time.
contrast: Doubles the t: gritted, gritting.

transitivity: both — transitive (*groped the wall for a switch*), intransitive (*groped in the dark*)
gloss: To feel around with your hands because you cannot see, or to touch someone sexually without their consent.
examples: I had to *grope* for the light switch in the dark hallway.
He *groped* his way down the basement stairs.
The witness said she was *groping* for the right word.

gloss: To earn a total amount of money before taxes and expenses are taken out.
examples: Sequels like this usually *gross* more overseas than at home.
The film *grossed* two hundred million dollars in three weeks.
The tour has *grossed* more than any other this year.
contrast: *Gross out* (to disgust) is a separate phrasal verb: *that video grossed me out*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*grunted an answer*), intransitive (*the pig grunted*)
gloss: To make a short, low sound in your throat, often instead of speaking.
examples: Teenagers sometimes just *grunt* instead of answering.
He *grunted* something and went back to his phone.
The weightlifter was *grunting* with every rep.

gloss: To laugh loudly and coarsely.
examples: Half the room will *guffaw* at that joke.
The audience *guffawed* at the senator's answer.
They were still *guffawing* when the lights came up.

gloss: To execute someone by cutting off their head with a guillotine.
examples: The revolutionaries would *guillotine* anyone they called an enemy.
They *guillotined* the king in January 1793.
Thousands had been *guillotined* by the end of the Terror.
contrast: The gu- is a hard g and the -ll- is a plain l: GIL-uh-teen.

ru: давить на совесть, заставлять чувством вины; пристыдить
gloss: To pressure someone into doing something by making them feel guilty.
examples: Don't let them *guilt* you into working the weekend.
She *guilted* her brother into driving her to the airport.
I'm tired of being *guilted* into covering other people's shifts.
contrast: Almost always with *into*: *guilt someone into doing something*.

gloss: To make a low bubbling sound, like water running through a narrow pipe.
examples: The radiators *gurgle* whenever the heat comes on.
The stream *gurgled* over the rocks behind the cabin.
The baby lay in her crib *gurgling* happily.

gloss: To take the insides out of a fish or animal, or to destroy the inside of a building or the substance of a law.
examples: You have to *gut* and clean the fish before you freeze it.
The fire *gutted* three floors of the warehouse.
The bill was *gutted* in committee.
contrast: Doubles the t: gutted, gutting.

transitivity: both — transitive (*guzzle a liter of soda*), intransitive (*he sat there guzzling*)
gloss: To drink or consume something quickly and greedily.
examples: Those old trucks *guzzle* gas.
He *guzzled* the whole bottle of water in one go.
The air conditioner has been *guzzling* electricity all summer.

gloss: To turn or swing around in fast circles.
examples: The dancers *gyrate* under the strobe lights.
The helicopter blades *gyrated* slowly to a stop.
Stock prices have been *gyrating* all week.
contrast: The g sounds like j: JY-rayt, not GY-rayt.

gloss: To make someone or something get used to a situation, so that it stops feeling strange.
examples: Short daily sessions *habituate* the dog to the crate.
Years abroad had *habituated* her to the cold.
The birds quickly became *habituated* to people.
contrast: Usually *habituate* someone **to** something.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the chatbot hallucinated a source*), intransitive (*the patient was hallucinating*)
gloss: To see or hear things that are not really there.
examples: High fevers can make small children *hallucinate*.
He *hallucinated* for two days after the surgery.
The model had *hallucinated* three citations that do not exist.

ru: делить пополам, разделить пополам; сокращать вдвое
transitivity: both — transitive (*halve the recipe*), intransitive (*sales halved*)
gloss: To cut something into two equal parts, or to reduce it to half its size.
examples: *Halve* the potatoes before you roast them.
The company *halved* its workforce in a single year.
Emissions have been *halved* since 2005.
contrast: The l is silent — *halve* sounds exactly like *have*: HAV.

ru: ставить в невыгодное положение, затруднять; мешать
gloss: To put someone at a disadvantage.
examples: Late funding will *handicap* the whole project.
Poor eyesight *handicapped* him for years.
Small farms are *handicapped* by the new labeling rules.
contrast: Doubles the p even though the stress is on the first syllable: handicapped, handicapping.

gloss: To choose someone or something personally and with great care.
examples: The founders *handpick* every new hire.
She *handpicked* the four people on her team.
The panel was *handpicked* by the governor's office.
contrast: Also written *hand-pick*; both spellings are common in American English.

gloss: To take place, especially without being planned.
examples: Things like that *happen* all the time around here.
Nobody could explain what *happened* that night.
It has *happened* twice this month already.
contrast: *Happen* is never passive: say *what happened?*, never *what was happened?*

gloss: To speak to someone at length in an angry, scolding way.
examples: He likes to *harangue* callers who disagree with him.
The coach *harangued* the team for twenty minutes.
She was *haranguing* shoppers from the sidewalk.
contrast: The final -ue is silent: huh-RANG; it drops before -ing — haranguing.

ru: жёстко встраивать, встроить; запрограммировать (в схему или в природу)
gloss: To build something in permanently, either into a machine's circuits or into someone's nature.
examples: Engineers *hardwire* the limit so that no one can change it later.
They *hardwired* the alarm into the building's power supply.
Humans seem to be *hardwired* to notice faces.
contrast: Also written *hard-wire*; the figurative sense is nearly always passive: *we're hardwired to...*

transitivity: both — transitive (*hasten the collapse*), intransitive (*I hasten to add*)
gloss: To make something happen sooner, or to hurry to say or do something.
examples: Cutting rates now could *hasten* a recovery.
The scandal *hastened* his resignation.
She *hastened* to add that nothing had been decided.
contrast: The t is silent: HAY-suhn.

gloss: To sell goods aggressively, often on the street or door to door.
examples: Vendors *hawk* bottled water outside the stadium.
He *hawked* cheap watches on the boardwalk all summer.
They have been *hawking* the same diet pills for years.

gloss: To offer a guess or an opinion even though you might well be wrong.
examples: I'd *hazard* a guess that half of them never read it.
She *hazarded* an opinion and was immediately shouted down.
No one has *hazarded* a firm estimate yet.

gloss: To force new members of a group through humiliating or dangerous initiation rituals.
examples: Some teams still *haze* their freshmen.
Two students said the fraternity *hazed* them for a week.
He was *hazed* so badly that he left the school.
contrast: Nothing to do with the noun *haze* (дымка); the -ing form *hazing* is the usual American word for the practice itself.

gloss: To have or place a company's main offices in a particular location.
examples: Insurers often *headquarter* their operations in Delaware.
They *headquartered* the new division in Austin.
The airline is *headquartered* in Atlanta.
contrast: Nearly always passive: *the firm is headquartered in Dallas*, not *the firm headquarters in Dallas*.

gloss: To pile something up, or to give someone a great deal of praise or blame at once.
examples: Critics *heap* praise on every record she puts out.
He *heaped* his plate with fries.
Blame was *heaped* on the contractor.
contrast: Often *heap* something **on** someone: *heaped scorn on the plan*.

ru: уклоняться от прямого ответа; страховаться, подстраховаться (от риска)
transitivity: both — transitive (*hedge their bets*), intransitive (*stop hedging and answer*)
gloss: To protect yourself against a possible loss, or to avoid answering a question directly.
examples: Airlines *hedge* against sudden jumps in fuel prices.
He *hedged* when reporters asked about the deadline.
The fund has been *hedging* its currency exposure all year.

gloss: To pay careful attention to advice or a warning and act on it.
examples: Few drivers *heed* the speed limit on that stretch.
The town *heeded* the evacuation order and got out early.
The engineers' warnings were never *heeded*.

ru: истекать кровью; терять в огромных количествах (деньги, сотрудников)
transitivity: both — transitive (*hemorrhaged cash*), intransitive (*the patient was hemorrhaging*)
gloss: To bleed heavily, or, of an organization, to lose money or people at a damaging rate.
examples: Without a transfusion a patient can *hemorrhage* to death in minutes.
The airline *hemorrhaged* cash for three straight quarters.
She was *hemorrhaging* internally by the time they operated.
contrast: American *hemorrhage*, British *haemorrhage*; note the double r, and the ending is just -ij: HEM-ur-ij.

gloss: To make sudden sharp sounds in your throat that you cannot control.
examples: Babies *hiccup* constantly in the first few weeks.
He *hiccuped* all through the ceremony.
She has been *hiccuping* for nearly an hour.
contrast: American spelling keeps one p — hiccuped, hiccuping; *hiccupped* and the old spelling *hiccough* are far less common.

gloss: To travel by standing at the roadside and getting free rides from passing drivers.
examples: Students still *hitchhike* to the coast in the summer.
He *hitchhiked* from Denver to Seattle in four days.
She spent that whole year *hitchhiking* around Europe.

ru: водить компанию (с влиятельными людьми), общаться запросто
gloss: To mix socially with important or wealthy people.
examples: Lobbyists *hobnob* with senators at these dinners.
He *hobnobbed* with the studio crowd all week.
She was *hobnobbing* with donors in the back room.
contrast: Doubles the b: hobnobbed, hobnobbing; always *hobnob* **with** someone.

gloss: To take or use all of something, leaving none for anyone else.
examples: Don't *hog* the remote all night.
One speaker *hogged* the entire discussion.
He has been *hogging* the good chair since he got here.
contrast: Doubles the g: hogged, hogging.

transitivity: both — transitive (*hollered a warning*), intransitive (*he hollered from the porch*)
gloss: To shout loudly, often to get someone's attention.
examples: Just *holler* if you need anything.
His father *hollered* at him from the driveway.
Somebody was *hollering* about a leak upstairs.

gloss: To make all the parts of something the same, or to treat milk so that the cream does not separate.
examples: Chain stores *homogenize* every downtown they move into.
The dairy *homogenized* and pasteurized the milk the same morning.
Television has *homogenized* regional accents.
contrast: American *homogenize*, British *homogenise*.

gloss: To take the vacation a couple goes on right after their wedding.
examples: They plan to *honeymoon* in Iceland.
My parents *honeymooned* in a borrowed cabin.
The couple are *honeymooning* somewhere in Portugal.

gloss: To trick someone by telling them something that is not true.
examples: These ads *hoodwink* people into signing long contracts.
The seller *hoodwinked* them about the condition of the roof.
Investors felt they had been *hoodwinked*.

gloss: To chase or pester someone constantly and without mercy.
examples: Reporters *hound* anyone connected to the case.
Collection agencies *hounded* him for two years.
She was *hounded* out of her job.

gloss: To make something feel more human, or to make people see someone as a real person.
examples: Small details *humanize* a story like this.
The documentary *humanized* a man most people knew only from headlines.
Critics say the film is *humanizing* a dangerous figure.
contrast: American *humanize*, British *humanise*.

gloss: To make someone feel less important or less proud, often by defeating them.
examples: One bad season can *humble* even a great team.
The loss *humbled* a squad that had not lost all year.
I was *humbled* by how much help people offered.
contrast: The b is silent: HUM-buhl.

transitivity: both — transitive (*hunch your shoulders*), intransitive (*he hunched over the desk*)
gloss: To bend your back and shoulders forward into a rounded shape.
examples: Don't *hunch* over your phone like that.
He *hunched* his shoulders against the wind.
Three of them were *hunched* around a laptop.

ru: нестись, мчаться; лететь на огромной скорости
gloss: To move very fast, usually in a way that looks out of control.
examples: Rocks sometimes *hurtle* down onto the highway here.
The truck *hurtled* through the intersection.
The country is *hurtling* toward another shutdown.
contrast: Not *hurdle* (барьер): a car *hurtles* down the road, a runner *hurdles* a barrier.

ru: глиссировать, скользить по воде; терять сцепление с мокрой дорогой
gloss: Of a vehicle, to slide out of control on a film of water lying on the road.
examples: Worn tires *hydroplane* easily in heavy rain.
The van *hydroplaned* and spun into the median.
She lost control after *hydroplaning* on a flooded curve.
contrast: American drivers say *hydroplane*; British drivers say *aquaplane*.

gloss: To promote something loudly and excessively in order to get attention for it.
examples: Studios *hype* every sequel as the biggest one yet.
The company *hyped* the launch for months.
The product was heavily *hyped* and then quietly canceled.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: hyping, not hypeing.

gloss: To put someone into a sleeplike state in which they respond to suggestion, or to hold their attention completely.
examples: Stage acts *hypnotize* volunteers from the audience.
The therapist *hypnotized* him as part of the treatment.
The children sat *hypnotized* by the fish tank.
contrast: American *hypnotize*, British *hypnotise*.

gloss: To think of someone or something as better or more perfect than they really are.
examples: We all *idealize* the decade we grew up in.
The movie *idealized* small-town life.
Their marriage has been *idealized* by everyone who writes about it.
contrast: American *idealize*, British *idealise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*imbibe the local customs*), intransitive (*they had been imbibing all evening*)
gloss: To drink something, especially alcohol, or to take in ideas from the world around you.
examples: Guests who *imbibe* should hand over their car keys.
He *imbibed* his father's politics without ever questioning them.
They had clearly been *imbibing* before the meeting.

gloss: To fill something or someone with a particular quality or feeling.
examples: A good teacher can *imbue* a class with real curiosity.
Her grandmother *imbued* her with a sense of duty.
The film is *imbued* with a quiet sadness.
contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: imbuing; usually *imbue* something **with** a quality.
